<explanation>
This project is an iOS UI component library – specifically, MessageKit – which provides a set of customizable components to build beautiful chat interfaces. Given that it is distributed as a Swift package with both the core library (under Sources) and an Example app demonstrating its use, your system design diagram should capture both the modular structure of the library itself and its interaction with a consuming application.

Here’s how to create an accurate and detailed system design diagram for MessageKit:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Library Modules:
     - Views: Includes all UI elements like message cells, avatars, bubbles, typing indicators, and accessory views. For instance, MessageContentCell and its subclasses (like TextMessageCell, MediaMessageCell, etc.) are central here.
     - Controllers: Comprises the message view controllers (e.g., MessagesViewController and its extensions for handling keyboard, pan gestures, typing indicator, etc.) which manage the messaging interface.
     - Layout: Contains layout calculators and flow layout classes (like MessageSizeCalculator, MessagesCollectionViewFlowLayout, etc.) that determine cell sizes and spacing.
     - Models & Protocols: Defines the data representations (e.g., MessageKind, Avatar, SenderType) and protocols that provide abstractions (e.g., MessagesDataSource, MessagesDisplayDelegate). This modularizes the behavior and interactions between the UI and data.
     - Supporting/Extensions: Includes helper methods and extensions for UIView, UIColor, NSAttributedString etc., to support customization and functionality.
   • Example Application:
     - This demo app is found in the Example folder. It integrates the MessageKit library into a practical messaging interface, wiring up sample controllers, custom layouts, and the usage of sample data.
   • Documentation & Resources:
     - Documents (such as the QuickStart and Custom Cells guidance) and assets (like images and storyboards) clarify design choices and help developers understand usage.

2. Define Relationships and Interactions:
   • Show how the MessageKit library exposes a set of protocols (data source, display delegate, layout delegate) that the consumer (the Example app or any end-user project) implements.
   • Draw directional arrows from the Example app (client) to the core library’s controllers, indicating “integration” and “delegation.”
   • Inside the library, demonstrate that the Controllers utilize Views and Layout modules – for instance, MessagesViewController querying the MessagesDataSource for message data to configure MessageContentCells, which in turn use Layout to size themselves.
   • Indicate that Models provide the data structure (such as MessageKind) that is used by Views to display message content, while Protocols enforce contract behavior.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns:
   • Modularity & Separation of Concerns:
       Each module – Views, Controllers, Layout, Models, and Protocols – is clearly separated. This follows an MVC/MVVM-like approach where user interface (Views) and business logic (Controllers and Models) are decoupled.
   • Delegation Pattern:
       Since MessageKit relies on delegate and data source protocols to abstract how messages are provided and rendered, show those interfaces with arrows pointing to their consumers.
   • Customization & Extensibility:
       Emphasize the extensible design (for example, the “custom” MessageKind) that allows end users to implement their own cells and behaviors.

4. Include Key Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Swift Package Manager is used to distribute the library.
   • Built for iOS (minimum iOS 14 for current versions) using Swift (Swift 6 or above for new versions).
   • Integration with third-party dependencies like “InputBarAccessoryView” which handles the input bar functionality.
   • Use of testing frameworks for unit tests and UI tests (as seen in the Tests and UITests folders).

5. Tailor the Diagram for a UI Component Library:
   • On one side, illustrate the “Core Library” with its modular components (Views, Controllers, Layout, Models, Protocols) and on the other, show how an “Application” (the Example app) consumes these modules.
   • Clearly label each component with its directory or role (e.g., Sources/Views, Sources/Controllers).
   • Use arrows to indicate data flow: from the Example app to MessagingViewController and on to MessageContentCells, which get layout information from Layout Calculators.
   • Emphasize the back-and-forth delegation calls, such as “MessageDataSource → provides messages” and “MessagesDisplayDelegate → customizes cell appearance.”

6. Practical Diagram Guidelines:
   • Use clear shapes with descriptive labels for each component. For example, rectangles for modules, ovals for protocols/interfaces, and containers for the Example app.
   • Include directional arrows to show dependencies and data flow. For example, show an arrow from the Example app’s messaging module to the MessageKit Controllers (indicating integration) and arrows from Controllers to Views and Layout.
   • Apply color coding to distinguish between different types of components – one color for core library modules, another for protocols/interfaces, and another for example/demo components.
   • Consider adding notes or callouts that mention important features (like customization of cells, integration of the InputBarAccessoryView, and support for various message types).

7. Final Checklist for the Diagram:
   - Clearly label each component (Core Library modules, Example app, external dependencies)
   - Use directional arrows to indicate data flow, delegation, and dependencies.
   - Apply color coding or distinct shapes to group related components.
   - Ensure that the diagram reflects modular separation (Views, Controllers, Layout, Models, and Protocols).
   - Capture integration points: how the Example app uses MessageKit and how customizations (e.g., custom MessageKind) are handled.

By following these guidelines, your system design diagram will accurately capture MessageKit’s distributed, modular architecture and communicate how the components work together to provide a customizable chat UI. This detailed depiction will allow developers and stakeholders to quickly grasp both the internal structure of the library and its usage in a real-world application context.
</explanation>
